tagline: Missouri River bluffs connect tribal communities, memorials and a changed shoreline
intro: Mixed-grass prairie, rolling hills and limestone river cliffs shape the Native American Scenic Byway through South Dakota. North Dakota’s section follows highways 1806 and 24 south from the Cannonball River. The Federal Highway Administration designates the route a National Scenic Byway, describing its memorials, museums and sacred sites as places to hear history from Native American perspectives. South Dakota’s tourism office traces its itinerary across the lands of the Yankton, Crow Creek, Lower Brule, Cheyenne River and Standing Rock Sioux Tribes.

The route crosses Big Bend Dam at Fort Thompson, a structure that changed the river and displaced communities. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers began construction in 1959; the dam created Lake Sharpe. Reservoir flooding displaced people on the Crow Creek and Lower Brule Reservations and submerged plants used for food and medicine.

Driving south from the Cannonball River brings you through Fort Yates and toward Kenel, then Mobridge and its Sitting Bull Monument. The South Dakota itinerary continues through the Eagle Butte and Fort Pierre areas to Big Bend Dam and Fort Thompson. Near Chamberlain, Dignity of Earth and Sky overlooks the Missouri; the state’s itinerary extends south to the Chief Standing Bear Bridge on the Nebraska border.

moments.title: Fort Yates
moments.text: Fort Yates is the headquarters of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe, on the western bank of Lake Oahe. The settlement developed after the U.S. Army established Standing Rock Cantonment here in 1863. The Army renamed the post Fort Yates in 1878 and decommissioned it in 1903. The fort also housed the headquarters of the U.S. Standing Rock Indian Agency. Sitting Bull was buried here, and a monument marks that burial site. The claim that his remains were moved to Mobridge in 1953 is disputed. The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe also founded Sitting Bull College in Fort Yates.

moments.title: Sitting Bull Monument
moments.text: Korczak Ziolkowski’s sculpture of Sitting Bull stands on the Standing Rock Sioux Reservation near Mobridge. The bust rests on a granite pedestal overlooking the Missouri River. The Dakota Memorial Association dedicated it on April 11, 1953. Claims that relatives and the association moved some or all of Sitting Bull’s remains here from Fort Yates that year remain disputed. Fort Yates has a separate monument at his burial site there.
moments.notice: The bust stands on a granite pedestal above the Missouri River.

moments.title: Dignity of Earth and Sky
moments.text: More than 100 blue diamond shapes make up the star quilt held by Dignity of Earth and Sky; they move in the wind. Dale Claude Lamphere’s 50-foot stainless steel sculpture depicts an Indigenous woman in Plains-style dress receiving the quilt. Lamphere says the work honors Lakota and Dakota cultures. Three Native American women from Rapid City served as models. Norm and Eunabel McKie announced the sculpture as a gift to South Dakota in 2014, honoring the statehood anniversary. Installed in September 2016, the statue overlooks the Missouri near Interstate 90 at Chamberlain.
